exercises.prompt:
What does this print?

```scala
val r =
  for
    x <- List(1, 2, 3)
    y <- List(10, 20)
    if x != 2
  yield x * y
println(r)
```
hints: For each `x`, the inner generator runs over both values of `y`.
The guard skips every combination where `x` is 2.
exercises.solution: The combinations in order are (1,10), (1,20), (2,10), (2,20), (3,10), (3,20). The guard drops those with `x == 2`. The products of the rest are 10, 20, 30, 60, and the result is a `List` because the first generator is a `List`: `List(10, 20, 30, 60)`.

exercises.prompt: You need an immutable sequence of a million measurements that you will index at random positions and occasionally append to. Which is the best default choice?

options.label: `Vector`
options.feedback: Yes. Indexing, updating and appending on a `Vector` are all effectively constant time.

options.label: `List`
options.feedback: Not yet. Indexing and appending on a `List` walk the list, so each costs time proportional to its length.

options.label: `Set`
options.feedback: Not yet. A set has no positions and removes duplicates, which would lose repeated measurements.

options.label: `LazyList`
options.feedback: Not yet. A `LazyList` is a lazy linked list: indexing is still linear.

hints: Look at the performance table: which immutable sequence has fast indexing?
exercises.solution: `Vector` is the general-purpose immutable indexed sequence, with effectively constant-time `apply`, `updated` and `:+`. A `List` would make each random access linear. If the code were local and performance-critical, an `Array` or `ArrayBuffer` would also be reasonable.

exercises.prompt: What are the keys of `List("kiwi", "fig", "plum", "pear", "date").groupBy(_.length)`? Enter each key.
hints: `groupBy` makes one key per distinct result of the function.
Count the letters of each fruit.
exercises.solution: The lengths are 4, 3, 4, 4, 4. `groupBy` creates one entry per distinct length, so the keys are 3 (`fig`) and 4 (the other four). The full map is `Map(3 -> List(fig), 4 -> List(kiwi, plum, pear, date))`, though the order in which a hash map prints its entries is not guaranteed.

exercises.prompt: Which expression does the compiler produce for `for x <- xs; y <- ys yield f(x, y)`?

options.label: `xs.flatMap(x => ys.map(y => f(x, y)))`
options.feedback: Yes. Every generator but the last becomes `flatMap`; the last becomes `map`.

options.label: `xs.map(x => ys.map(y => f(x, y)))`
options.feedback: Not yet. That would produce a collection of collections; `flatMap` flattens it.

options.label: `xs.zip(ys).map((x, y) => f(x, y))`
options.feedback: Not yet. `zip` pairs elements at the same position; a for comprehension combines every `x` with every `y`.

options.label: A `while` loop over indexes
options.feedback: Not yet. For comprehensions are translated into method calls, which is why they work on any type with `map` and `flatMap`.

hints: The result should be flat: one element per pair (x, y).
exercises.solution: The translation is `xs.flatMap(x => ys.map(y => f(x, y)))`. Guards would add `withFilter` calls. Because only these methods are needed, the same syntax works for `Option`, `Either`, `Future` and any type you define with `map` and `flatMap`.
